1.text:
How Did We Figure Out That Earth Moves?

Try this right now: can you feel Earth moving? Nobody can. You're spinning with the planet and racing around the Sun at the same time, and it feels like sitting perfectly still. That's exactly the problem ancient astronomers faced.

This deck tells one of my favorite stories in science. People started with a model where Earth sat motionless at the center of everything. Over many centuries, they moved to a model where Earth is just one planet circling the Sun. Telescope evidence backed it up, and one law of gravity finally tied the whole thing together.

The story didn't really end until 1838, when someone measured a tiny shift in a star that the Greeks had searched for and never found. If you keep one idea from this deck, make it this one: scientific models change when new observations arrive.

Did you know? The doodle in the corner shows Jupiter with four little moons. Galileo spotted those moons in 1610, and you'll see why they mattered later in this deck.

2.text:
Does the Sun Move Across the Sky, or Do We?

Every morning the Sun rises in the east, and every evening it sets in the west. But what's really going on?

Here are your choices. A) The Sun circles Earth every day. B) Earth spins once every day. C) You can't tell just by looking.

Vote, and then defend your choice. Then try the harder part: what evidence could you show someone who picked a different answer?

3.text:
Today I Can...

Here's the plan for this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can check yourself at the end.

I can explain retrograde motion two ways, Ptolemy's and Copernicus's. I can tell how Tycho, Kepler, and Galileo changed the model. I can use P² = a³ to find a planet's year or distance. I can explain an orbit as falling around Earth, the way Newton did. I can draw how the Moon's pull makes two tidal bulges. And as a bonus, I can explain how parallax proved Earth moves, thanks to Bessel.

Each one is tagged with an Indiana standard: ES.2.5, ES.2.4, or ES.4.7. The last one is extra enrichment. You'll rate yourself 1 to 3 on each at the end.

4.text:
Part 1: Earth at the Center

Think of two everyday things that make it seem like Earth isn't moving. Maybe you thought of this: you don't feel any wind from racing through space. Or this: a ball you drop falls straight down. The star patterns look the same year after year, too.

For nearly 1,900 years, the Earth-centered model was the accepted picture of the universe. Aristotle laid out its ideas around 350 BC, and Ptolemy turned it into precise math around 150 AD. In this part we'll ask why a still Earth made so much sense, and why smart, careful observers held onto it for so long.

5.text:
The Geocentric Model

In the geocentric model, Earth sits still at the center, and everything else circles it. Moving outward, you'd find the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Beyond all of them was a giant sphere carrying the "fixed" stars.

Aristotle had physics reasons for this. Heavy things fall toward the center of the universe, he said, and that's why they fall toward Earth. And if Earth really moved, we'd feel it, and we'd see the stars shift. The heavens were thought to be perfect and unchanging, so objects up there moved in perfect circles.

Around 150 AD, Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, turned all this into a detailed mathematical model in a book called the Almagest.

Did you know? Geocentric does not mean flat. Educated Greeks knew Earth was a sphere. Aristotle pointed to Earth's curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses.

6.text:
Retrograde Motion

Watch Mars night after night, and you'll usually see it creep slowly eastward against the background stars. But every so often, Mars does something odd. It slows down, stops, and drifts backward, westward, for several weeks. Then it stops again and goes back to moving east, tracing a loop in the sky.

That backward drift is called retrograde motion. For Mars it happens about every 26 months and lasts about 2 months. Jupiter and Saturn do it every year. On the slide, east is on the left, just like the real sky when you face south, so Mars's usual path runs right to left with the loop in the middle.

That puts every model of the solar system on the spot: if planets really move in circles, how could one go backward? The next slides give two very different answers.

Did you know? The word planet comes from the ancient Greek planetes, which means "wanderer."

7.text:
Ptolemy's Way: Epicycles

Ptolemy had a clever fix that kept Earth still and orbits circular. Each planet rides on a small circle called an epicycle. The center of that small circle travels around Earth on a big circle called the deferent.

Picture a carnival ride where your seat spins in a little circle while the whole arm swings you around a big one. Most of the time, the two motions add up, and the planet moves forward. But when the planet swings around the inner side of its epicycle, it moves the opposite way for a while, and from Earth it looks like it loops backward. Those loops are retrograde motion.

And it worked. It predicted planet positions within a few degrees and was used for about 1,400 years. A model can be useful and still be wrong about what's actually happening.

8.text:
Why It Lasted

Here's a big reason the Earth-centered model held on: stellar parallax. Hold your thumb out at arm's length and blink one eye, then the other. Your thumb jumps against the far wall. If Earth really went around the Sun, a nearby star should shift the same way between January and July, compared to more distant stars.

The Greeks looked carefully and saw zero shift. That left two choices: either Earth doesn't move, or the stars are unimaginably far away. The second one seemed ridiculous, so most people chose the first.

But the stars really are that far. Even the nearest star shifts by less than 1 arcsecond, about 1/1,800 of the full Moon's width. That's far too small to see without a telescope. The model also kept making good predictions, and a model that works is hard to give up. (Remember, the drawing isn't to scale!)

Did you know? Around 270 BC, a Greek named Aristarchus of Samos suggested the Sun was at the center. The missing parallax was a strong scientific argument against him.

9.text:
Check for Understanding: Ptolemy's Mars

Let's see if Ptolemy's model makes sense to you. In his Earth-centered model, what makes Mars seem to move backward?

Is it A) Mars rides around its epicycle, B) Earth passes Mars on the inside track, C) Mars stops and reverses its orbit, or D) clouds block our view of Mars?

Careful: one of these is a correct idea from a different model. Pick the one that fits Ptolemy's model and be ready to explain your choice.

10.text:
Copernicus

Part 2 starts here, with the Sun at the center. Over about 80 years, three people turned the picture inside out: Copernicus, Tycho Brahe, and Kepler.

In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish church official and astronomer, published his big book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. He died that same year. In his model, the Sun sits at the center, and Earth is just a planet. It spins once a day and goes around the Sun once a year. He also put the planets in the right order with the right relative distances.

But Copernicus held onto one old idea: heavenly motion had to be perfect circles. Real orbits aren't circles, so he still needed small epicycles to match the data, and his model predicted planet positions no better than Ptolemy's. That's why it didn't win people over right away. (This drawing isn't to scale, either.)

Did you know? Copernicus proposed that Earth moves and showed it could work, but he didn't prove it. The evidence came later from Kepler, Galileo, Newton, and finally Bessel in 1838.

11.text:
Copernicus's Way

In the Sun-centered model, retrograde motion is an illusion caused by our own motion. Earth is on the inside track, closer to the Sun, and it moves faster. It goes around once a year, while Mars takes 1.88 years.

Think of a race where you're on the inside lane and pass a slower runner. For a moment, that runner seems to slide backward against the trees behind them. Follow the numbered sight lines on the slide. From positions 1 to 3, Mars seems to move forward against the stars. From 3 to 5, Earth passes Mars and the sight line swings back, so Mars appears to go backward. From 5 to 7, it moves forward again.

No loop in the orbit itself is needed. Mars never actually goes backward. We just see it from a moving planet.

Did you know? You can see the same effect on a highway. Pass a slower car, and it seems to slide backward against distant hills.

12.text:
Tycho Brahe's Data

Tycho Brahe was a Danish nobleman who built the best observatory of his time, and he did it all before telescopes existed. With huge instruments like his giant wall quadrant, he measured star and planet positions night after night for more than 20 years.

His precision was about 1 arcminute. The full Moon is about 30 arcminutes wide, so Tycho could measure angles to about 1/30 of the Moon's width with his bare eyes. That was several times better than anyone before him.

Tycho never saw stellar parallax either, so he came up with his own model: the Sun and Moon circle a still Earth, while the other planets circle the Sun. In 1600 he hired a young mathematician named Johannes Kepler. After Tycho died in 1601, Kepler got to work on his data.

Did you know? Tycho showed that a "new star" in 1572 (a supernova) and a comet in 1577 were farther away than the Moon. So the heavens weren't unchanging after all.

13.text:
Kepler's First Law

Kepler spent years trying to make circles fit Tycho's Mars data. His best circle model still missed by up to 8 arcminutes. That sounds tiny, but Kepler trusted Tycho's 1-arcminute data more than the ancient idea of perfect circles. So he threw the circles out.

Kepler's first law: each planet orbits in an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus. An ellipse is a stretched circle with two special points inside called foci. The Sun sits at one of them, and the other one is empty. The distance labeled a on the slide is the semi-major axis, half the long width of the ellipse.

The drawing is stretched so you can see the idea. Real planet orbits are nearly circles. A number called eccentricity measures the stretch. A circle has e = 0, Earth's orbit has e = 0.017, and Mars's has e = 0.094.

Did you know? Kepler published this in 1609 in a book called Astronomia Nova, which means "New Astronomy."

14.text:
Kepler's Second Law

Kepler's second law says a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Imagine a line stretching from the Sun to the planet. As the planet moves, that line sweeps across space like a windshield wiper.

Look at the two colored wedges. Each one took one month, and they have the same area. Near the Sun, the wedge is short, so it has to be wide: the planet is moving fast. Far from the Sun, the wedge is long, so it has to be thin: the planet is moving slowly.

So planets don't cruise at a steady speed. Earth goes about 30.3 km/s in early January, when it's closest to the Sun, and about 29.3 km/s in early July, when it's farthest.

Did you know? It's like a figure skater who spins faster when pulling their arms in. Newton later showed this law comes from the same physics.

15.text:
Kepler's Third Law

Kepler's third law is short enough to fit on a sticky note: P² = a³. P is a planet's year, measured in Earth years, and a is its average distance from the Sun, measured in AU.

Let's test it. For Earth, a = 1 AU and P = 1 year, and 1 squared equals 1 cubed. For Mars, a = 1.52 AU, so a³ is about 3.51, and P = 1.88 years, so P² is about 3.53. Jupiter, at 5.20 AU, takes 11.86 years, and both sides come out to about 140. It checks out.

The pattern: farther planets are slower and have longer years. Their path is longer, and they move more slowly along it. Watch your units, though. This simple form only works in years and AU.

Did you know? Kepler published this law in 1619. Newton later upgraded it into a version that works for any orbiting pair, which lets astronomers weigh the Sun and planets.

16.text:
Activity: Draw an Ellipse

Time to draw an orbit yourself. Push 2 pins into a piece of cardboard, 8 cm apart. Loop a string around both pins, and pull it tight with a pencil. Keeping the string tight, trace all the way around. Ta-da: an ellipse!

Now redraw it with the pins 4 cm apart, then 12 cm apart. Label one pin "Sun" on each drawing.

But predict first: what shape will you get if both pins go in the same hole? Then, for each drawing, find the eccentricity: e = (pin gap) ÷ (long axis).

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Asteroid Year

Here's a chance to use Kepler's third law. An asteroid orbits 4 AU from the Sun. How long is its year?

Is it A) 4 years, B) 8 years, C) 16 years, or D) 64 years?

Write out P² = a³ and plug in the number one step at a time. Each wrong answer is waiting for a common slip.

18.text:
Venus's Phases

Part 3 starts here: evidence and gravity, from Galileo to Newton. This is the observation that ruled out Ptolemy.

In Ptolemy's model, Venus always stays between Earth and the Sun. That means we'd only ever see its mostly dark side, so Venus would only show crescent and new phases. But in late 1610, Galileo pointed his telescope at Venus and saw a full set of phases, including nearly full. Venus also changed size: small and nearly full when it was on the far side of the Sun, and big and crescent when it was on our side. That only works if Venus goes around the Sun.

Careful, though: this didn't prove Earth goes around the Sun. Tycho's hybrid model, where planets circle the Sun while the Sun circles Earth, also predicts a full set of phases. So Venus knocked out Ptolemy, but Copernicus and Tycho were both still standing.

Did you know? The direct evidence that Earth moves came much later, from a discovery about starlight in 1729 and Bessel's parallax in 1838.

19.text:
Galileo's Telescope

Galileo didn't invent the telescope, but in 1609 he built better ones, up to about 20 to 30 times magnification. Between 1609 and 1613, his observations showed that the heavens weren't perfect at all.

He saw mountains and craters on the Moon, so it was a rough, Earth-like world, not a perfect ball. He found four moons circling Jupiter, not Earth. That proved not everything goes around us, and it showed a moving planet can keep its moons. And he saw sunspots moving across the Sun, which showed that the Sun has spots and rotates.

None of these alone proved the Sun-centered model, but together they broke the old idea of perfect, unchanging heavens centered on Earth. His 1632 book led to a trial in 1633, where he was found "vehemently suspected of heresy" and kept under house arrest for the rest of his life. The Church formally admitted its error in 1992.

Did you know? Even Galileo got things wrong. His theory of the tides blamed the sloshing of oceans on Earth's motion and rejected any role for the Moon. Newton would show otherwise.

20.text:
Newton's Gravity

In 1687, Isaac Newton published a book called the Principia, and in it his law of universal gravitation: every mass pulls on every other mass. The formula is F = Gm₁m₂/d². Here m₁ and m₂ are the two masses and d is the distance between them.

Bigger masses pull harder. Double one mass, and the force doubles. Distance matters even more. Move twice as far away, and the pull drops to 1/4. G is a tiny number, which is why you don't feel the pull of the person sitting next to you.

Newton also wrote three laws of motion. Put them together with gravity, and all three of Kepler's laws pop right out. Kepler described how planets move. Newton explained why. (The picture isn't to scale!)

Did you know? Newton's third law says pulls come in equal pairs. Earth pulls on a falling apple, and the apple pulls back on Earth just as hard.

21.text:
Newton's Cannonball

Newton imagined a cannon on top of a very tall mountain, firing sideways. Gravity pulls the ball down, while its speed carries it forward. Fire it slowly, and it lands nearby. Fire it faster, and it lands farther away. Faster still, and it lands farther yet.

Now fire it at about 8 km/s. The ground curves away beneath the ball just as fast as it falls, so it keeps falling and keeps missing. That's an orbit! An orbit is falling around Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

The Moon is a cannonball too, always falling toward Earth while moving sideways. That's how Newton connected a falling apple to the Moon's orbit. And astronauts on the ISS float because they're falling right along with their station, not because gravity is gone.

Did you know? Fire the cannonball at about 11 km/s and it would escape Earth completely.

22.text:
Gravity Makes Tides

Newton's gravity explains the tides too. Gravity weakens with distance, so the Moon pulls hardest on Earth's near side, a little less on Earth's center, and weakest on the far side. You can see it on the slide: strong, medium, weak.

That difference stretches Earth's oceans. The water on the near side gets pulled toward the Moon, and the water on the far side gets "left behind." So there are two bulges, two high tides on opposite sides, with low tides in between. (The bulges are exaggerated so you can see them.)

As Earth spins under the bulges, most coasts get two high tides and two low tides every 24 hours and 50 minutes. The Sun makes tides too, a little less than half as strong as the Moon's. The Sun has about 27 million times the Moon's mass, but it's about 390 times farther away. Tides depend on mass divided by distance times distance times distance (distance cubed), so the Sun's great distance almost cancels out its great mass.

Did you know? This is the same idea you saw in Deck 2. What's new here is that one law of gravity explains it all.

23.text:
Check for Understanding: Draw It

Now it's your turn to be the scientist. Draw the Sun, the Moon, and Earth's two bulges for a spring tide (new or full Moon) and a neap tide (quarter Moon).

In each drawing, label high tide and low tide, and add arrows showing the Sun's and Moon's pulls.

Think about where the Moon has to be in each case, and how that changes the shape of the water.

24.text:
How Science Changes Its Mind

A scientific model is our best explanation, and it gets revised when new data arrive. Follow the timeline like a chain of clues. Around 150 AD, Ptolemy's epicycles fit what people could see with their eyes. In 1543, Copernicus put the Sun at the center. In the 1570s, Tycho collected precise data. In 1609, Kepler swapped circles for ellipses. In 1610, Galileo saw Venus's phases and Jupiter's moons. In 1687, Newton explained it all with gravity.

The last stop is 1838. Using a precision telescope, Friedrich Bessel finally measured the yearly back-and-forth shift of a star called 61 Cygni: about 0.3 arcseconds. That's the parallax the Greeks couldn't see. It was the proof the Greeks had been looking for that Earth orbits the Sun, and it gave the first distance to a star: about 10 light-years by Bessel's measurement (today's value is about 11.4).

The Greeks weren't wrong to look for parallax. They were only wrong about how far away the stars are. It took about 300 years after Copernicus, and much better instruments, to see it. And remember: the old model wasn't useless. It was a good model for the data of its time.

Did you know? Today the Gaia spacecraft measures parallaxes for over a billion stars.

25.text:
Newton's Math Finds a Planet

This is where Newton's gravity earned its keep. Astronomers noticed that Uranus was drifting off the path that Kepler's laws and Newton's gravity predicted. Something was tugging on it.

A mathematician named Le Verrier used gravity math to predict where an unseen planet must be. In 1846, the astronomer Galle pointed a telescope at that spot, and there it was: Neptune.

Look at the slide: the predicted path and the actual path don't match, and that mismatch was the clue. A good model doesn't just explain what we've seen. It predicts things we haven't seen yet.

26.text:
Exit Ticket

You just covered more than 2,000 years of science. Show what you've got with three quick questions.

First, explain Mars's backward loop two ways: Ptolemy's and Copernicus's. Second, a planet's year is 8 years. How far is it from the Sun? Third, Venus shows a full set of phases. Which model does that rule out, and why wasn't it final proof?

When you're done, flip your card over and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each "I can" statement from Slide 3.

27.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus to stretch your thinking. How did Newton's gravity find Neptune before anyone saw it?

Look back at Slide 25, and explain it as if you were telling a friend who missed class.

28.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.2.5: explain how scientific ideas change as new information and observations come in. Use the work of Ptolemy, Copernicus, Brahe, Kepler, and Galileo to show how data and scientific discussion changed our understanding of how the solar system moves.

ES.2.4: use math or computer models to show how planets, moons, comets, and asteroids move, and explain that Kepler's laws come straight from Newton's law of gravity and his laws of motion. ES.4.7: make diagrams or models showing how the Sun's and Moon's gravity pull on Earth's oceans, explain the difference between daily tides (high and low) and monthly tides (spring and neap), and explain how the monthly tides follow the Moon's trip around Earth, and so its phases.
